arXiv:2610.18694v1 [cs.CV] 13 Oct 2026

GeoReader: Learning Latent Geometry for
Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models

Abstract

Vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with metric and multi-view relationships that remain implicit in RGB observations. Geometry foundation models recover this structure from RGB, but existing methods either fuse the estimated features with visual tokens and learn to use them from question answering alone, or align VLM latents with geometry features. Capturing geometry, however, does not ensure its use: zeroing the aligned latents of a released feature-alignment model leaves its accuracy unchanged. We introduce GeoReader, a framework that learns geometric representations for the VLM that reads them. First, we train lightweight Geometric Readers to produce continuous input tokens, supervising them with geometry descriptions decoded by a frozen VLM, so that the Readers express geometry in a form the target model can already read. We then freeze the Readers to preserve this interface while fine-tuning the VLM on spatial QA, with geometry injection conditioned on the question. Geometry descriptions serve only as training targets: at inference, the VLM answers directly from the continuous geometric tokens without generating a geometry chain of thought. With geometry predicted from RGB images, GeoReader reaches 94.394.3 on MindCube-Tiny with Qwen3-VL-4B and, with a multi-source QA mixture, an average of 72.572.5 across six additional spatial benchmarks with Qwen3.5-9B. These results suggest that a useful geometric representation is one the receiving model can use, not merely one from which geometry can be reconstructed.

1 Introduction

Vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated increasingly strong capabilities in general multimodal understanding, yet continue to struggle with spatial reasoning, a capability essential to embodied intelligence in the 3D world [Li et al., 2025a; Hu et al., 2026a]. A central challenge is inferring and reasoning about 3D structure from 2D observations [Li et al., 2025b], as required by spatial questions involving camera motion, viewpoint changes, and object distances. Recent advances in geometry foundation models [Wang et al., 2025a; Lin et al., 2026] offer a promising opportunity to address this limitation by providing geometry information. How to harness this information for VLM spatial reasoning has therefore become an important question.

Existing approaches to integrating geometry foundation models with VLMs have improved spatial reasoning and can be broadly categorized into two streams. The first introduces geometry as an additional input modality [Fan et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2025a; Zhao et al., 2026], fusing features from geometry foundation models with the VLM’s original visual features (Fig. 1a). This provides a direct way to incorporate geometry into existing VLMs, and the VLM learns to use these features from downstream supervision. However, this supervision alone may not teach the VLM to interpret geometry features. The second uses geometry as supervision, typically by aligning VLM latent representations with features from geometry foundation models [Chen et al., 2026] (Fig. 1b). This encourages the latent space to capture geometry information while preserving the VLM’s input and output interfaces. Nevertheless, capturing geometry does not ensure its use: zeroing the latents of the released first-stage 3DThinker [Chen et al., 2026] checkpoint leaves MindCube-Tiny [Wang et al., 2026a] accuracy essentially unchanged, and answer tokens barely attend to them (; ). Related analyses of latent visual reasoning methods such as LVR [Li et al., 2026a] and Monet [Wang et al., 2026b] also highlight a disconnect between intermediate representations and answer generation [Viveiros et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026d; Zhu et al., 2026; Park et al., 2026]. Despite their differences, neither approach explicitly bridges the gap between geometry representations and language-grounded spatial relations for VLMs. Consequently, the role of geometry information in the model’s reasoning remains uncertain. We bridge this gap by converting geometry into a form that VLMs can both interpret and ground in language.

We introduce GeoReader, based on the core idea that geometry should first be converted into a form that VLMs can interpret as spatial relationships in language, before VLMs learn to use it for downstream tasks. To this end, a two-stage pipeline separates adapting geometry to the VLM from applying it to spatial QA (Fig. 1c). In Stage 1, we train lightweight Geometric Readers to convert per-view geometric signals into continuous geometric tokens. These tokens and the corresponding images are given to a frozen VLM that predicts geometry descriptions. With the VLM frozen, this supervision trains the Readers to express geometry information in a form that the model can interpret through its existing language capabilities. In Stage 2, we transfer the pretrained Readers to spatial QA, freezing the Readers to preserve their learned mapping while fine-tuning the VLM to use their outputs. Since questions differ in how much they rely on each geometric signal, a geometry injector conditions on the images and question to set each signal’s strength. Geometry descriptions are used only for Stage 1 supervision; at inference, the VLM answers directly using the geometric tokens.

We evaluate GeoReader across seven spatial reasoning benchmarks and three VLM families. With geometry predicted from RGB images, GeoReader achieves 94.3%94.3\% accuracy on MindCube-Tiny with Qwen3-VL-4B and, with multi-source QA training, an average accuracy of 72.5%72.5\% across six additional benchmarks with Qwen3.5-9B (Sec. 4.2). Comparisons with vanilla supervised fine-tuning (SFT) under matched QA data and training settings show gains concentrated on questions requiring metric 3D understanding. Ablations further show the benefits of readability pretraining, freezing the Readers during downstream adaptation, and the geometry injector (Secs. 4.3 and 4.4). Geometry interventions show that the model uses the supplied geometry: in a controlled MindCube-Tiny experiment with annotation-derived camera geometry, removing geometry content reduces accuracy from 89.2%89.2\% to 77.2%77.2\%, while shuffling poses across views reduces it to 63.1%63.1\%.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose explicitly connecting geometry information to spatial relationships expressed in language, separating adapting geometry to the VLM from applying it to spatial reasoning.

  • •

    We introduce GeoReader, a two-stage framework that trains lightweight Geometric Readers through language supervision from a frozen VLM, then freezes the Readers and adapts the VLM for spatial QA with question-conditioned geometry injection (Sec. 3).

  • •

    We demonstrate the effectiveness of GeoReader across seven spatial reasoning benchmarks and three VLM families, with ablations and geometry interventions supporting both the framework’s design and the model’s use of geometry information (Secs. 4.2–4.5).

2 Related Work

Spatial reasoning in vision-language models.

SpatialVLM [Chen et al., 2024], SpaRE [Ogezi and Shi, 2025] and SPAR-7M [Zhang et al., 2025] build synthetic or 3D-grounded spatial QA data. SpatialLadder [Li et al., 2026c] and HiSpatial [Liang et al., 2026] organize training from perception toward reasoning, while SenseNova-SI [Cai et al., 2026] studies scaling spatial data. SpatialQA [Cai et al., 2025] and ViewSpatial [Li et al., 2026b] target depth and viewpoint relations; N3D-VLM [Wang et al., 2025c] links 3D object localization to reasoning. These works establish the value of spatial supervision; we study how to present estimated geometry to the answering VLM.

Geometry-augmented VLMs.

DUSt3R [Wang et al., 2024] and MASt3R [Leroy et al., 2024] estimate point maps and correspondences; CUT3R [Wang et al., 2025b] maintains a recurrent scene state. VGGT [Wang et al., 2025a] predicts camera and dense geometry, and Depth Anything V2 [Yang et al., 2024] and Depth Anything 3 [Lin et al., 2026] predict depth and any-view geometry. Geometry-augmented VLMs take such 3D structure as input: 3D-LLM [Hong et al., 2023] and LEO [Huang et al., 2024] ground language in 3D scenes. LLaVA-3D [Zhu et al., 2025], Video-3D LLM [Zheng et al., 2025b] and SR-3D [Cheng et al., 2026] add spatial positions or regions to visual inputs. SpatialRGPT [Cheng et al., 2024], SD-VLM [Chen et al., 2025] and HiSpatial [Liang et al., 2026] use relative depth, depth positional encoding and metric point maps, respectively. VLM-3R [Fan et al., 2026], Spatial-MLLM [Wu et al., 2025a] and VG-LLM [Zheng et al., 2025a] fuse visual and 3D features; SpaceMind [Zhao et al., 2026] uses camera-guided fusion, and SpatialStack [Zhang et al., 2026a] spreads geometry across LLM layers. These studies vary the geometric source and fusion; we train the interface for the receiving VLM.

Learning geometry representations for reasoning.

G2VLM [Hu et al., 2026b] combines reconstruction with spatial understanding, and GAP-MLLM [Zhang et al., 2026b] pretrains with sparse point-map and semantic prediction. SpatioLM [Wu et al., 2026] uses pseudo depth and camera supervision but only RGB at inference; GeoSR [Zhang et al., 2026c] finds that fused VGGT tokens are often underused and masks visual tokens during training to force their use, with QA as the only supervision. 3DThinker [Chen et al., 2026] aligns generated latents with VGGT features, and CoVT [Qin et al., 2026] learns continuous visual thoughts; LVR [Li et al., 2026a] and Monet [Wang et al., 2026b] reason with visual latents, and Coconut [Hao et al., 2025] reasons in a continuous latent space. Unlike these methods, GeoReader supervises its geometric input through description prediction by the frozen VLM, and takes estimated pose and depth, not descriptions, at inference.

3 Method

We aim to supply a pretrained VLM with geometric input that meets two separate requirements: the geometric tokens must be readable by the receiving model, and the model must use them for the question at hand. GeoReader addresses them with two training stages (Fig. 2). After the preliminaries (Sec. 3.1), we describe how a Geometric Reader encodes each view as a geometric token (Sec. 3.2), how Stage 1 trains it for readability through the frozen VLM (Sec. 3.3), and how Stage 2 injects these tokens according to the question (Sec. 3.4).

3.1 Preliminaries

A VLM with parameters θ\theta encodes the VV images I={Ii}i=1VI=\{I_{i}\}_{i=1}^{V} into visual tokens X1,…,XVX_{1},\ldots,X_{V}, embeds the question as text tokens QQ, and feeds the sequence of dd-dimensional embeddings to a language model that predicts the answer aa with next-token distribution pθp_{\theta}. Each view ii also has geometric signals GimG^{m}_{i}, m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M}, here camera pose relative to view 1 and a depth map; the formulation applies to any per-view signal. We turn GmG^{m} into additional tokens of this input sequence.

3.2 Geometric Token Encoding

To feed geometry through the VLM’s existing input channel, a lightweight Geometric Reader EmE_{m} maps each view of signal mm to one continuous input embedding. For view ii, it first computes per-patch descriptors Uim∈ℝNim×cmU^{m}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{i}^{m}\times c_{m}} on the same patch grid as the RGB tokens; each cmc_{m}-dimensional descriptor holds the patch position together with pose-related quantities or depth statistics of that patch. A learned query 𝐫m\mathbf{r}^{m} then reads only that view’s descriptors:

Mmi=MLPm(LN(Umi)),Zmi=Decm(𝐫m,Mmi)∈ℝ1×d,Zm=Em​(Gm)=[Z1m;…;ZVm]∈ℝV×d,\begin{gathered}M^{m}_{i}=\mathrm{MLP}_{m}\bigl(\mathrm{LN}(U^{m}_{i})\bigr),\qquad Z^{m}_{i}=\mathrm{Dec}_{m}\bigl(\mathbf{r}^{m},M^{m}_{i}\bigr)\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times d},\\ Z^{m}=E_{m}(G^{m})=\bigl[Z^{m}_{1};\ldots;Z^{m}_{V}\bigr]\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times d},\end{gathered} (1)

where Decm\mathrm{Dec}_{m} applies two Transformer decoder blocks with 𝐫m\mathbf{r}^{m} cross-attending to MimM^{m}_{i}, then a linear projection. We call ZmZ^{m} geometric tokens: continuous embeddings, one per view in input-view order. The Reader encodes geometry alone; the VLM combines it with RGB through its own attention layers. Each signal has its own Reader, so signals keep their own structure (Sec. A.2.1).

3.3 Frozen-VLM Readability Training

QA supervision alone does not specify what the geometry encodes, and feature alignment measures similarity to an external target rather than what the receiving VLM can read (Sec. 1). We instead supervise each Reader through the frozen target VLM: given the images, the geometric tokens and a fixed instruction, the VLM predicts a geometry description ymy^{m} of signal mm with teacher forcing. For two ScanNet [Dai et al., 2017] views, the camera description reads “compared with image 1, the observer in image 2 moves 0.4 meters right and 0.1 meters backward, and turns left by about 23 degrees,” and the depth description lists objects per view, e.g., “guitar (left) at 1.7 meters.” The supervised positions 𝒯m\mathcal{T}^{m} cover geometric content such as distances, directions and angles; template words, predictable without geometry, are excluded. The description loss is

ℒreadm=−1|𝒯m|∑t∈𝒯mlogpθ(ytm∣I,Zm,y<tm),θfrozen,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{read}}^{m}=-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}^{m}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}^{m}}\log p_{\theta}\bigl(y^{m}_{t}\mid I,Z^{m},y^{m}_{<t}\bigr),\qquad\theta\ \text{frozen}, (2)

where gradients pass through the frozen VLM to update only EmE_{m}. This trains the Reader to produce geometric tokens readable by the VLM, with descriptions used only as training targets.

Pair-supervised readability.

Descriptions of a signal such as camera pose relate each view to reference view 1. Group supervision supervises the descriptions of all VV views jointly in one example; the description of view ii can then be predicted from any view’s tokens, so the loss does not tell the Reader which token should carry that relation. Pair supervision removes this ambiguity by applying Eq. 2 to each reference–target pair: for target view i∈{2,…,V}i\in\{2,\ldots,V\}, the Reader encodes only the geometry of views 1 and ii, and the frozen VLM predicts view ii’s description relative to view 1 from these two views, so only their tokens can explain it. Stage 2 inputs keep all views (Sec. A.1.1).

3.4 Question-Conditioned Geometry Injection

Freezing the Readers.

Stage 2 supervises answers, which do not explicitly require the Readers to retain the geometric relationships specified by the Stage 1 descriptions. Updating the Readers under this supervision may weaken their ability to express geometry beyond what the training questions need. We therefore freeze the Readers and adapt the VLM to this fixed interface.

Question-conditioned readout.

Questions differ in how much they rely on each geometric signal, so we let the question set each signal’s strength. We compute it from the final-layer hidden state of the last valid question token, which attends to all preceding visual and question tokens and thus summarizes the task context. Geometric embeddings, however, enter before layer 1, and one forward pass cannot use its own final-layer state to set earlier inputs. We therefore first run a read pass over only the images and question to obtain this hidden state, hqh_{q}, before adding geometry.

Geometry injector.

A geometry injector turns the frozen Reader outputs into the geometric tokens of the answer pass. For each signal mm, it maps ZmZ^{m} through an adapter PmP_{m}, scales the result by a gate computed from hqh_{q} with a routing head RmR_{m}, and adds it to the slot embeddings Bm∈ℝV×dB^{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times d}, the learned input embeddings of the placeholder tokens at the geometric-token positions:

Z~m=Bm+gm​Pm​(Zm),gm=sigmoid⁡(Rm​(hq)).\widetilde{Z}^{m}=B^{m}+g_{m}P_{m}(Z^{m}),\qquad g_{m}=\mathrm{sigmoid}\bigl(R_{m}(h_{q})\bigr). (3)

The adapter fits the frozen Reader outputs to the VLM, and gmg_{m} is the question-dependent strength of signal mm. If a signal is missing (e.g., inter-view geometry for one image), gm=0g_{m}=0 and the slot embeddings alone mark it as absent, keeping the layout unchanged.

Training and inference.

The answer pass places Z~m\widetilde{Z}^{m} after the question, so the passes encode

Sread=[X1,…,XV,Q],Sans=[X1,…,XV,Q,{Z~m}m∈ℳ,a],S_{\mathrm{read}}=\bigl[X_{1},\ldots,X_{V},Q\bigr],\qquad S_{\mathrm{ans}}=\bigl[X_{1},\ldots,X_{V},Q,\{\widetilde{Z}^{m}\}_{m\in\mathcal{M}},a\bigr], (4)

where aa is the ground-truth answer in training and is generated at inference. Both passes share the VLM parameters, and we stop gradients through the read pass to save memory and computation. We fine-tune the language model and the geometry injector with next-token cross-entropy on the answer and keep the Readers and the vision encoder frozen. Since the geometric tokens come after the question, SansS_{\mathrm{ans}} begins with SreadS_{\mathrm{read}}; at inference, the answer pass reuses the read pass’s key–value cache and computes only the geometric tokens and the answer.
